## Development validation

This vignette accompanies development version 0.99.1.
The benchmark covers selected configurations, and the validation study uses
100 datasets per metric with 99 resampling draws. These small simulations
provide diagnostics; they do not establish general statistical calibration.
The local study observed 24% peak false positives, 10% peak detection,
74.9% transfer interval coverage, and 43% drift interval coverage in the
tested scenarios. These results limit inferential use of these methods. Report sources are `scripts/benchmark.R` and `scripts/validate.R`.

## The pseudo-replication problem

Most biological measurements are taken on a small number of biological units
(animals, cell cultures, donor samples), each measured several times. The
several-per-unit measurements are technical replicates. They share instrument
noise and sample-handling artefacts with the other measurements on the same
unit, so they are correlated. Treating them as independent inflates the apparent
sample size and shrinks the standard error by roughly a factor of
`\sqrt{k}`, where `k` is the number of technical replicates per biological unit.

This is the standard pseudo-replication failure described by Vaux, Fidler and
Cumming (2012). It is the single most common statistical mistake in biological
experimental data reported in experimental practice. crossStatR makes the correct workflow the
default: pass a `bio_rep` identifier (and optionally a `tech_rep` identifier)
to `sci_describe()`, and the function averages the technical replicates within
each biological unit before computing summary statistics or fitting tests.

The example uses a small dose-response example that resembles
an enzyme-kinetics assay. The example simulates three biological replicates per dose
condition, with two technical replicates per biological unit. The two technical
replicates share a biological-unit-level random effect so they are positively
correlated.

## Simulating a dose-response experiment

```{r sim-data}
set.seed(101)
doses <- c(0, 1, 5, 25)              # µM, nominal
n_bio <- 6                            # biological replicates per dose
n_tech <- 2                           # technical replicates per bio unit
mu <- c(2.0, 2.6, 3.4, 4.0)           # true means per dose
sigma_bio <- 0.25                     # between-bio SD
sigma_tech <- 0.07                    # within-bio, between-tech SD

rows <- list()
for (d in seq_along(doses)) {
  for (b in seq_len(n_bio)) {
    bio_effect <- rnorm(1, mean = mu[d], sd = sigma_bio)
    for (t in seq_len(n_tech)) {
      rows[[length(rows) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
        dose = doses[d], dose_f = factor(doses[d]),
        bio = paste0("d", d, "_b", b),
        tech = t,
        y = bio_effect + rnorm(1, sd = sigma_tech)
      )
    }
  }
}
df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
head(df, 4)
```

## Descriptive statistics at the right level

The correct call averages technical replicates within each biological unit
before computing per-dose means and standard errors:

```{r describe}
desc <- sci_describe(df$y, group = df$dose_f,
                    bio_rep = df$bio, tech_rep = df$tech)
print(desc)
```

The reported `n` per dose is 6, the number of biological replicates. The
standard error is the between-bio-unit standard error. Compare this with
the naive call that ignores the replicate structure:

```{r describe-naive}
naive <- sci_describe(df$y, group = df$dose_f)
print(naive)
```

The naive call reports `n = 12` per dose. The standard error is roughly
half of the correct value, because it confuses within-bio noise with
between-bio variation. Any p-value computed downstream from the naive summary
will be far too small.

The documentation does not recommend reporting the naive summary in a paper, even as a
supplementary table. The temptation to compare the two summaries and pick the
one that supports the hypothesis is exactly the kind of analysis-decision
sensitivity that `experiment_fragility()` is designed to expose (see the
*Advanced Uncertainty Attribution* vignette).

## Plotting the data honestly

A honest plot shows each biological replicate as a point (after averaging its
technical replicates) and overlays the group mean. Plotting all 24 raw points
as if they were independent is the visual analogue of pseudo-replication.

```{r plot-data, fig.cap = "Dose-response with biological replicates shown as points (technical replicates pre-averaged). Black diamonds are group means; error bars are 95% CIs on the mean."}
bio_means <- aggregate(y ~ dose_f + bio, data = df, FUN = mean)
group_summary <- desc$summary
group_summary$dose_f <- factor(group_summary$group)

ggplot(bio_means, aes(x = dose_f, y = y)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(data = group_summary,
                  aes(y = mean, ymin = mean_ci_low, ymax = mean_ci_high),
                  colour = "black", size = 0.6, fatten = 2.5,
                  shape = 18) +
  labs(x = "Dose (µM)", y = "Response (a.u.)",
       title = "Dose-response: 6 biological replicates per dose") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Two-group comparison

To compare two dose levels the example calls `sci_compare()`. The default test is
Welch's t, which the example prefers over Student's t in essentially all experimental
settings because the equal-variance assumption rarely holds. If the
distributions are visibly non-Gaussian (small `n`, heavy tails), use the
permutation test instead; it does not require a Gaussian null and it controls
Type I error under exchangeability.

```{r compare}
sub <- df[df$dose %in% c(1, 5), ]
bio_means2 <- aggregate(y ~ dose_f + bio, data = sub, FUN = mean)
x <- bio_means2$y[bio_means2$dose_f == "1"]
y <- bio_means2$y[bio_means2$dose_f == "5"]
sci_compare(x, y, test = "welch")
```

The example deliberately computes the comparison on the per-bio-unit means rather than
on the raw 12-row subset. The two-level averaging (technical replicates
within bio units, then compare bio means) is what justifies the Welch test's
independence assumption.

## ANOVA across all doses

A one-way ANOVA across all four doses asks whether the means differ
anywhere. The example uses the default `aov` path with Tukey HSD post-hoc and
report the effect-size estimates.

```{r anova}
bio_means_all <- aggregate(y ~ dose_f + bio, data = df, FUN = mean)
fit <- sci_anova(y ~ dose_f, data = bio_means_all,
                posthoc = "tukey")
print(fit)
```

The `effect_sizes` table reports eta-squared, partial eta-squared, and
omega-squared. The example prefers omega-squared for one-way designs because it is
less biased upwards in small samples (Kelley, 1935; Carroll and Nordholm,
1975). The Levene's test p-value is reported so the analyst can decide whether to
refit with `welch = TRUE`; if the variances look equal across groups the
classic F-test is fine, and if they do not, refit:

```{r anova-welch}
fit_w <- sci_anova(y ~ dose_f, data = bio_means_all, welch = TRUE)
print(fit_w)
```

## Effect size with confidence interval

A p-value alone is uninformative about the magnitude of the difference. The example
recommends reporting a standardised effect size alongside the test. For the
two-group comparison above:

```{r effect-size}
sci_effect_size(x, y, type = "cohens_d")
sci_effect_size(x, y, type = "hedges_g")
```

The Hedges' `g` applies a small-sample bias correction to Cohen's `d`. For
`n = 6` per group, the correction is roughly 6%, which is large enough to
matter. The example prefers `g` for small samples and `d` for sample sizes above
roughly 20 per group.

## When the design is more complex

If the biological units are themselves clustered (mice within a cage, cells
within a passage, donor samples within a batch), the simple average-then-test
workflow above is no longer adequate because it ignores the cluster-level
correlation. Use `replicate_decompose()` instead. It fits a linear mixed
model with `lme4::lmer` and reports variance components for each level of
replication.

If the analyst wants to attribute variance across several experimental stages
(sampling, instrument noise, calibration, drift), see the
*Advanced Uncertainty Attribution* vignette. The Category C functions
`uncertainty_origin()` and `drift_uncertainty()` are designed for that
question.

## What to take away

Three things. First, average technical replicates within biological units
before any inferential statistics; `sci_describe()` does this for the analyst when
the analyst supplies `bio_rep` and `tech_rep`. Second, default to Welch's t unless the analyst
have a stated reason to use Student's, and use the permutation test when
the Gaussian assumption is doubtful. Third, report effect sizes with
confidence intervals, not just p-values, and prefer Hedges' `g` for small
samples.

## References

- Carroll, R. M. and Nordholm, L. A. (1975). Sampling characteristics of Kelley's epsilon-squared and Hays' omega-squared. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 35, 541-554. [Source](https://doi.org/10.1177/001316447503500304).

- Kelley, T. L. (1935). An Unbiased Correlation Ratio Measure. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 21, 554-559. [Source](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.21.9.554).

- Vaux, D. L., Fidler, F. and Cumming, G. (2012). Replicates and repeats—what is the difference and is it significant? The EMBO Reports, 13, 291-296. [Source](https://doi.org/10.1038/embor.2012.36).
